p.src: Now Sun the Great Sage had exhausted all his ingenuity in asking the Tathagata to subdue the monsters and deliver Tripitaka and his disciples from peril. They left Lion-Camel City and journeyed westward. After several more months, winter was already upon them. And this was what they saw:

p.src: Master and disciples pressed on through bitter cold, lodging in the rain and taking their meals in the wind. As they traveled, another walled city came into view. Tripitaka asked, “Wukong, what place is that ahead?” The Pilgrim replied, “We shall know when we reach it. If it is the seat of a western king, we must have our travel document countersigned; if it is merely a prefecture, department, or county, we shall pass straight through.”

p.src: Before master and disciples had finished speaking, they had already arrived outside the city gate. Tripitaka dismounted, and the company of four entered the outer ward. They saw an old soldier sleeping beneath a sunlit wall, curled up out of the wind. The Pilgrim went up, shook him once, and called, “Officer.” The old soldier awoke with a start and opened his bleary eyes. Seeing the Pilgrim, he hastily fell to his knees, knocked his head on the ground, and cried, “Grandfather!” The Pilgrim said, “Do not make such a foolish commotion. I am no evil deity. Why do you call me grandfather?” Kowtowing, the old soldier said, “You are Grandfather Thunder God.” “Nonsense,” said the Pilgrim. I am a monk traveling from the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven in quest of scriptures. We have only just arrived and do not know the name of this place, so I came to ask you.” Only then did the old soldier recover his composure. He yawned, scrambled to his feet, stretched, and said, “Venerable sir, venerable sir, please forgive this humble man. This country was originally called the Kingdom of Bhikshus, but it is now called the City of Children.” The Pilgrim asked, “Does the country have an emperor?” The old soldier replied, “Yes, yes, yes.” The Pilgrim turned to the Tang Monk and said, “Master, this place was originally the Kingdom of Bhikshus and is now called the City of Children, though I do not know why its name was changed.” Puzzled, the Tang Monk said, “If it is called Bhikshu, why is it also called Children?” Bajie said, “I expect the King of Bhikshus died and the newly enthroned king is a child; hence the name City of Children.” The Tang Monk said, “That cannot be right, that cannot be right. Let us go in and ask again in the streets.” Sha Monk said, “Precisely. For one thing, that old soldier does not know; for another, Elder Brother frightened him into talking nonsense. Let us enter the city and make inquiries.”

p.src: They passed through three more gates and reached the broad thoroughfares and great marketplace. The people were indeed neatly dressed and fair in appearance. And this was what they saw:

u.src: They passed through three more gates and reached the broad thoroughfares and great marketplace. The people were indeed neatly dressed and fair in appearance.
And this was what they saw:

p.src: The four travelers led the horse and carried the luggage through the marketplace for a long while. Its splendor seemed inexhaustible, yet at every household doorway they saw a goose cage. Tripitaka said, “Disciples, why does every household here place a goose cage before its door?” Hearing this, Bajie looked from side to side. They were indeed goose cages, each screened by curtains of colored silk. The fool laughed and said, “Master, perhaps today is an auspicious day for marriages and meeting friends, and they are all exchanging gifts.” The Pilgrim said, “Nonsense! How could every household be exchanging gifts at once? There must be some reason for this. Wait while I go forward and look.” Tripitaka caught hold of him and said, “Do not go. Your face is ugly, and I fear you will alarm them.” The Pilgrim said, “I shall transform myself before I go.”

p.src: The worthy Great Sage formed a spell with his fingers, recited an incantation, shook himself, and changed into a honeybee. Spreading his wings, he flew near, slipped behind a curtain, and looked inside. There, as it happened, sat a small boy. He went to look in the cage at the second house, and there too was a small boy. He looked in eight or nine houses in succession, and every cage held a small boy. All were male; there was not a single girl. Some sat playing in their cages, while others sat inside crying; some ate fruit, while others slept or merely sat. When the Pilgrim had finished looking, he resumed his true form and reported to the Tang Monk, “There are children in those cages. The oldest are not yet seven, and the youngest are only five. I do not know why they are there.” On hearing this, Tripitaka was filled with uncertain misgivings.

p.src: Turning into another street, they suddenly saw a government office: it was the Golden Pavilion Post Station. The elder rejoiced and said, “Disciples, let us go into this post station: first, to ask about the place; second, to feed and settle the horse; and third, since evening is coming, to find lodging.” Sha Monk said, “Quite right, quite right. Let us go in quickly.” The four entered cheerfully. The resident official, who was indeed the postmaster, received them at the gate, and they exchanged greetings. After they had taken their seats and exchanged courtesies, the postmaster asked, “From where have you come, venerable sir?” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk was sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. Now that we have reached your esteemed country, our travel document must duly be inspected. Meanwhile, we beg leave to rest awhile in your honorable office.” The postmaster immediately ordered tea to be served. When they had finished their tea, he arranged provisions and ordered the attendants on duty to prepare their hospitality. Tripitaka thanked him and then asked, “May we enter the court today, have audience with His Majesty, and submit our travel document for inspection?” The postmaster replied, “It cannot be done tonight. You must wait until tomorrow’s morning court. For tonight, please make yourselves comfortable in this humble office.”

p.src: Before long, when all was ready, the postmaster invited the four pilgrims to share the vegetarian meal. Then he ordered his men to clean the guest rooms for them to rest in. Tripitaka thanked him profusely. Once they were seated, the elder said, “There is something I do not understand and would like to ask you about. Please enlighten me. How are children raised and treated in your country?” The postmaster replied, “There cannot be two suns in heaven, nor two different principles among men. Children are conceived from the father’s essence and the mother’s blood, carried in the womb for ten months, and born when their time comes. After birth they are nursed for three years and gradually grow into their proper form. How could anyone not know that?” Tripitaka said, “By your account, it is no different from my own country. Yet when I entered the city, I saw every household along the streets keeping a child hidden inside a goose cage. I do not understand this, and so I venture to ask.” The postmaster leaned close to his ear and whispered, “Elder, do not concern yourself with it, ask about it, heed it, or speak of it. Please retire now and continue your journey tomorrow morning.” Hearing this, the elder seized the postmaster by the arm and insisted on learning the truth. The postmaster shook his head and wagged a finger, saying only, “Guard your tongue.” Tripitaka clung to him all the more stubbornly and demanded every detail. Helpless, the postmaster dismissed all the attendants and officials present. Alone with him beneath the lamplight, he whispered, “The matter of the goose cages that you asked about arises from the wickedness of our present sovereign. Why must you keep asking about it?” Tripitaka asked, “In what way is he wicked? You must explain it clearly before I can set my mind at ease.” The postmaster said, “This country was originally called the Kingdom of Bhikṣu, but a recent folk rhyme has renamed it the City of Children. Three years ago, an old man dressed as a Daoist arrived with a young girl who was just sixteen. The girl was exquisitely beautiful, with a face like Guanyin’s. He presented her to the reigning king, who delighted in her beauty, took her into his favor at the palace, and titled her the Beautiful Queen. Of late he will not even look properly at the ladies of the Three Palaces or the consorts of the Six Courts. Day and night, he gives himself endlessly to pleasure. Now his vitality is exhausted, his body wasted and feeble; he scarcely eats, and his life may end at any moment. The Imperial Medical Academy has exhausted every good prescription but cannot cure him. The Daoist who presented the girl received an imperial title from our lord and is called the Royal Father-in-Law. The Royal Father-in-Law possesses a secret prescription from beyond the seas, said to be wonderfully effective in prolonging life. Not long ago he went to the Ten Continents and Three Isles to gather the ingredients, and everything is now prepared. But the medicine requires a dreadful catalyst: the hearts and livers of exactly one thousand one hundred and eleven children must be decocted into a broth with which to take it. Once taken, it is said to keep a man from aging for a thousand years. The children in those goose cages have all been selected and are being kept inside them. Their parents, terrified of the king’s law, dare not even weep; thus the folk have spread the name City of Children. When you attend court tomorrow morning, Elder, only exchange your travel document. You must not mention this matter.” With that, he withdrew.

Because you craved pleasure and beauty until you made yourself ill, how can you unjustly sacrifice the lives of so many children? What misery! What misery! My heart is breaking!” A poem bears witness to this. The poem says:

p.src: Bajie stepped forward and said, “Master, what has come over you? You are forever carrying someone else’s coffin into your own house to mourn over it. Do not distress yourself. As the saying goes, ‘If a sovereign orders his minister to die, the minister who refuses is disloyal; if a father orders his son to perish, the son who refuses is unfilial.’ It is his own subjects he is harming. What has it to do with you? Come, loosen your clothes and sleep. Do not borrow troubles from people of old.” Tripitaka said through his tears, “Disciple, you are devoid of compassion. We who have left the household accumulate merit and cultivate conduct; our foremost duty is to aid others. How can this foolish king behave so wantonly? Never has it been known that eating human hearts and livers can prolong life. Faced with such a thing, how could I not grieve?” Sha Monk said, “Master, do not grieve yet. Tomorrow morning, after exchanging the travel document, speak to the king face-to-face about it. If he refuses to listen, we shall see what manner of man this Royal Father-in-Law is. Perhaps the Royal Father-in-Law is a monster who craves human hearts and livers and has devised this scheme for that very purpose. We cannot know.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “Wujing speaks sense. Master, sleep for now. Tomorrow I shall go to court with you and find out whether the Royal Father-in-Law is good or evil. If he is human, I fear only that he has strayed into heterodox practices, knows nothing of the true Way, and blindly takes the gathering of medicines for truth. In that case, I shall teach him the essential principle of the innate Way and convert him to the right path. If he is an evil monster, I shall seize him and show him to the king, then make the king curb his desires and nurture his health. I will never allow him to take the lives of those children.” Hearing this, Tripitaka hurriedly bowed and, in turn, saluted Pilgrim, saying, “Disciple, your proposal is excellent, truly excellent. But when we meet the foolish king, we must not ask about this matter at once. I fear he will disregard friend and stranger alike, condemn us for spreading rumors, and hold us guilty. What would we do then?” Pilgrim laughed. “I have powers of my own. First I shall spirit the children in the goose cages out of the city, so that tomorrow there will be none from whom to take hearts. The local officials will naturally memorialize the throne. That foolish king will surely issue an order, consult the Royal Father-in-Law, or command that other children be selected and reported. At that moment we can use the occasion to make our report, and no blame can possibly fall upon us.” Tripitaka was delighted. Then he asked, “But how can the children be taken out of the city now? If you truly can deliver them, worthy disciple, your virtue will be as vast as heaven. Do it quickly. If you delay even a little, I fear it may be too late.” Pilgrim roused his divine might, rose at once, and instructed Bajie and Sha Monk, “Remain seated here with Master while I work my art. As soon as you feel a dark wind blowing, you will know that the children have left the city.” All three chanted together, “Homage to the Medicine Buddha who saves living beings! Homage to the Medicine Buddha who saves living beings!”

p.src: The Great Sage went outside, gave a shrill whistle, and rose into midair. Forming a hand-sign and reciting an incantation, he cried, “Om, Pure Dharma Realm!” He thereby summoned the City God, the local earth gods, the gods of the soil, the divine officials, the Guardians of the Five Directions, the Merit Officers of the Four Watches, the Six Ding and Six Jia spirits, the guardian devas of the Teaching, and all the rest. They gathered in the sky, saluted him, and asked, “Great Sage, why have you summoned us by night? What urgent business is there?” Pilgrim said, “We are now passing through the Kingdom of Bhikṣu, whose wicked king has believed an evil monster and intends to use children’s hearts and livers as a medicinal catalyst in the hope of attaining longevity. My master cannot bear it and wishes to save the children and destroy the monster. Therefore I have specially invited you all to exercise your divine powers and help me transport every child in every household’s goose cage throughout the city—cage and all—to hollows in the hills or deep within the forests outside the city. Hide them there for a day or two and give them fruit to eat, so that none suffers from hunger. Protect them secretly as well, and do not let them become frightened or cry. After I have destroyed the evil, set the country in order, and persuaded the king to return to righteousness, bring them back to me before I depart.”

p.src: At daybreak, Tripitaka awoke, dressed himself fully, and said, “Wukong, I shall take advantage of the early court audience and go have our travel document endorsed.” Monkey said, “Master, I fear you will accomplish nothing if you go alone. Let me go with you and see whether that Father of the Queen is righteous or wicked.” Tripitaka said, “But if you go, you will refuse to observe the proper courtesies, and I fear the king will take offense.” Monkey said, “I shall remain invisible and follow you secretly, serving as your guard.” Tripitaka was delighted. After instructing Bajie and Friar Sand to guard the luggage and horse, he set off. Tripitaka said, “But if you go, you will refuse to observe the proper courtesies, and I fear the king will take offense.”
Monkey said, “I shall remain invisible and follow you secretly, serving as your guard.”
Tripitaka was delighted. After instructing Bajie and Friar Sand to guard the luggage and horse, he set off.
The posthouse master came to see him again and found the elder, now fully attired, looking even more remarkable than the day before.
This was his appearance:

p.src: After the posthouse master had exchanged courtesies with him, he whispered in his ear, warning him only not to meddle in other people’s affairs. Tripitaka nodded his assent. The Great Sage slipped beside the gate, recited a spell, shook himself, and changed into a tiny insect. With a hum, he flew onto Tripitaka’s hat. They left the posthouse and headed straight for the royal court.

p.src: On reaching the palace gate, Tripitaka saw a chamberlain and saluted him, saying, “This humble monk was sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. Now that I have reached your honored realm, I must duly have my travel document endorsed. I wish to appear before His Majesty, so I humbly beg you to announce me.” The chamberlain duly conveyed his request. The king said with delight, “A monk who has come from afar must possess spiritual attainment.” He ordered that Tripitaka be invited in. Receiving the royal command, the chamberlain led the elder inside. After the elder had paid homage below the steps, he was invited into the hall and granted a seat. The elder thanked the king for his favor and sat down. The king looked emaciated and feeble, his spirits weary: when he raised his hands, his gestures of courtesy went awry; when he spoke, his voice came in broken phrases. The elder presented his travel papers. The king’s eyes were dim and clouded; only after looking them over again and again did he take up the royal seal, affix his endorsement, and hand them back to the elder. The elder received them.

p.src: The king was greatly delighted by what he heard. All the officials at court cheered, crying, “Splendid—‘The Way alone is honored above all! The Way alone is honored above all!’” Seeing everyone praise the Daoist, the elder was overcome with shame. The king then ordered the Court of Imperial Entertainments to prepare a vegetarian meal for the monk from afar before he departed westward from the city. Tripitaka thanked him for his favor and withdrew. He had only just descended from the hall and was walking out when Monkey flew down from the crown of his hat and called into his ear, “Master, that Father of the Queen is an evil fiend, and the king has been afflicted by his demonic aura. Go back to the posthouse and wait for the meal. Old Monkey will stay here and listen for news of his plans.” Tripitaka understood and left the palace gate alone. Of him we shall speak no more for now.

p.src: As for Monkey, with a flutter of his wings he flew to the emerald screen in the Golden Throne Hall and clung there. He saw an officer of the Five-City Military Command step out from among the ranks and report, “My sovereign, during the night a blast of cold wind swept away the children kept in goose cages in every ward and household, cages and all. Not a trace of them remains.” Hearing the report, the king was both shocked and vexed. He said to the Father of the Queen, “This must be Heaven’s destruction of me. I have been gravely ill for months, and the imperial physicians have been powerless. Fortunately, Your Excellency bestowed an immortal prescription upon me, and we were only awaiting noon today to cut the children open and take their hearts and livers as the medicinal catalyst. Who could have expected the cold wind to sweep them away? If this is not Heaven’s will to destroy me, what is it?” The Father of the Queen laughed and said, “Your Majesty, pray do not distress yourself. The children’s disappearance is precisely Heaven’s way of granting Your Majesty longevity.” The king asked, “The children in the cages have plainly been swept away. How can you say instead that Heaven is granting me longevity?” The Father of the Queen replied, “When I came to court just now, I saw a most excellent medicinal catalyst, far superior to the hearts of those one thousand one hundred and eleven children. Those children’s hearts could extend Your Majesty’s life by only a thousand years; but if this catalyst is taken with my immortal medicine, it can extend your life for countless ages.” The king had no idea what this medicinal catalyst might be and questioned him repeatedly. Only then did the Father of the Queen say, “That monk sent from the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures—I observed that his bearing is pure and his features perfectly formed. He possesses the true body of one who has cultivated himself through ten incarnations. A monk since childhood, he has never dissipated his primal yang, making him ten thousand times superior to those children. If we could obtain his heart and liver, boil them into a broth, and take it with my immortal medicine, it would assuredly preserve Your Majesty’s life for ten thousand years.” The benighted ruler believed every word. He said to the Father of the Queen, “Why did you not tell me sooner? If it is truly so effective, we should have detained him just now instead of letting him leave.” The Father of the Queen said, “What difficulty is there in that? You ordered the Court of Imperial Entertainments to prepare a vegetarian meal for him. He will certainly eat before leaving the city. Issue an urgent decree now: have every gate shut tight, muster troops to surround the Golden Pavilion Posthouse, and bring the monk here. We must first courteously ask him to give up his heart. If he consents, cut it out at once; afterward, give his corpse an imperial burial and even build him a temple where sacrifices may be offered. If he refuses, then treat him to force rather than courtesy: bind him immediately, cut him open, and take it. What difficulty could there be?” The benighted ruler followed his advice and immediately issued a decree to close every gate. He also dispatched officers and soldiers of every rank from the Feathered Forest Guard to surround the posthouse.

p.src: When Pilgrim heard this news, he flew swiftly back to the posthouse, resumed his true form, and said to the Tang Monk, “Master, disaster has struck! Disaster has struck!” Tripitaka had just received the imperial meal with Eight Rules and Friar Sand when he suddenly heard these words. He was so terrified that his three vital spirits scattered and smoke seemed to pour from his seven apertures; he collapsed in the dust, drenched in sweat, his eyes staring blankly and his tongue unable to speak. In alarm, Friar Sand hurried forward to support him, calling again and again, “Wake up, Master! Wake up, Master!” Eight Rules said, “What disaster is it? What disaster is it? You could have told us more slowly instead of frightening Master into such a state.” Pilgrim said, “After Master left the court, I stayed behind to watch and discovered that the royal father-in-law is a fiend. Presently, officers of the Five-City Military Command came to report that a cold wind had swept away the children. The king was just becoming angry when the fiend instead told him to rejoice, saying, ‘This is Heaven sending you the means to immortality.’ He means to take Master’s heart and liver as the guiding ingredients of a medicine that will prolong the king’s life for ten thousand years. That foolish ruler believed his slanderous words, so he has mustered elite troops to surround the posthouse and sent an Embroidered-Uniform officer to summon Master and demand his heart.” Eight Rules laughed and said, “A fine act of mercy you performed, a fine rescue of the children, and a fine dark wind you raised—and now you’ve brought disaster down upon us.”

p.src: Trembling all over, Tripitaka struggled to his feet, clutched Pilgrim, and pleaded piteously, “Worthy disciple, what are we to do about this?” Pilgrim replied, “If you want matters put right, we must make the great small.” Friar Sand asked, “What do you mean by ‘make the great small’?” Pilgrim said, “If we are to save your life, the master must become the disciple and the disciple the master. Only then can you be kept safe.” Tripitaka said, “If you can save my life, I would gladly become your disciple—or even your disciple’s disciple.” Pilgrim said, “If that is so, we must not delay.” He ordered, “Eight Rules, quickly mix up some mud.” The idiot at once used his rake to break up some earth. Not daring to go outside for water, he lifted his clothes, urinated on it, mixed a lump of stinking mud, and handed it to Pilgrim. Having no other choice, Pilgrim flattened the mud into a sheet, pressed it onto his own face, and fashioned a mask in the likeness of a monkey’s face. He told the Tang Monk to stand up, keep still, and say nothing. He stuck the mask onto the Tang Monk’s face, recited a true spell, breathed a mouthful of immortal breath, and cried, “Change!” The elder immediately changed into Pilgrim’s likeness. They removed his clothes and dressed him in Pilgrim’s garments. Pilgrim, meanwhile, put on his master’s robes, formed a hand seal, recited an incantation, shook himself, and changed his face into that of the Tang Monk. Even Eight Rules and Friar Sand could not tell them apart.

p.src: Just as they finished arranging the disguise to their satisfaction, they heard gongs and drums sounding together and saw a dense throng of spears and swords approaching. It was an officer of the Imperial Guard, who had led three thousand soldiers to surround the posthouse. Then an Embroidered-Uniform officer entered the posthouse courtyard and asked, “Where is the elder from the Tang realm in the East?” Terrified, the postmaster knelt trembling and pointed, saying, “In the guest room down there.” The Embroidered-Uniform officer immediately went to the guest room and said, “Elder Tang, my king summons you.” Eight Rules and Friar Sand stood on either side, guarding the false Pilgrim. The false Tang Monk came through the door, saluted, and said, “My lord of the Embroidered Uniform, why has His Majesty summoned this poor monk?” The Embroidered-Uniform officer stepped forward, seized him, and said, “Come to court with me.
